### Pre-submission checks

- [x] I am **not** reporting a bug (crash, false positive/negative, etc). These must be filed via the bug report template.
- [x] I have looked through both the [open](https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+) and [closed](https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20state%3Aclosed) issues for a duplicate request.
- [x] I affirm that I have followed the [AI policy](https://github.com/zizmorcore/.github/blob/main/AI_POLICY.md) and that this request constitutes my own words and understanding.

### What's the problem this feature will solve?

(This is basically #2057, but opened to track and discuss adding support for specific package managers).

#2061 introduced the `adhoc-packages` audit for detecting ad-hoc installation or invocation of packages via RubyGems and npm. Scope for the initial PR was deliberately kept small to these ecosystems to allow for reviewability, but the underlying scope of #2057 is of course broader; many package managers support one-off installation or execution patterns that bypass committed dependency state, lockfiles, and hash verification.

This is similar in shape to `use-trusted-publishing`; the high-level security concern is ecosystem-independent, but accurate detection requires package-manager-specific handling.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Extend `adhoc-packages` audit to various other popular ecosystems.

Listed below are a few specific command shapes for some ecosystems/package managers that I've identified as candidates likely worth flagging, but happy to split these out into separate issues or organize however maintainers prefer!

| Ecosystem | Command shape | Category | Caveats |
|---|---|---|---|
| JavaScript | `pnpm dlx <pkg>`, `pnpx <pkg>`, `pnx <pkg>` | Ad-hoc package execution |  |
| JavaScript | `yarn dlx <pkg>` | Ad-hoc package execution |  |
| Python | `pip install <requirement>`, `python -m pip install <requirement>` | Direct package installation | Omit local package installs (`.`, `./pkg`, `../pkg`) and requirements files (`-r <file>`). |
| Python | `uv pip install <requirement>` | Direct package installation | Omit local package installs (`.`, `./pkg`, `../pkg`) and requirements files (`-r <file>`). |
| Python | `uvx <tool>`, `uv tool run <tool>` | Ad-hoc tool execution |  |
| Python | `uv tool install <tool>` | Ad-hoc tool installation |  |
| Python | `uv run --with <requirement> ...` | Ad-hoc package execution | Omit local package inputs (`.`, `./pkg`, `../pkg`). |
| Python | `pipx run <app>` | Ad-hoc tool execution | Omit local package inputs (`--path`, `.`, `./pkg`, `../pkg`). |
| Python | `pipx install <app>` | Ad-hoc tool installation | Omit local package inputs (`.`, `./pkg`, `../pkg`). |
| Rust | `cargo install <crate>` | Ad-hoc tool installation | Omit `--path <path>`; that installs a local crate rather than resolving one from a registry/git source. |
| Rust | `cargo binstall <crate>` | Ad-hoc binary/tool installation |  |
| Go | `go install <module/cmd>@<version>` | Ad-hoc tool installation | Require the `@<version>` query; without it, `go install` runs in the current module/workspace context. |
| Go | `go run <module/cmd>@<version>` | Ad-hoc tool execution | Require the `@<version>` query; omit local package/file targets such as `.`, `./cmd/foo`, `*.go`. |
| .NET | `dotnet tool install --global <pkg>`, `dotnet tool install -g <pkg>` | Ad-hoc tool installation |  |
| .NET | `dotnet tool install --tool-path <path> <pkg>` | Ad-hoc tool installation |  |
| .NET | `dotnet tool install <pkg>`, `dotnet tool install --local <pkg>` | Local tool manifest mutation | Flag install/mutation; omit `dotnet tool restore` and `dotnet tool run`, which use the committed local tool manifest. |
| PHP | `composer require <pkg>` | Project dependency addition |  |
| PHP | `composer global require <pkg>` | Ad-hoc tool installation |  |

As mentioned in previous discussions, exact top-level versions reduce risk across ecosystems, but they do not necessarily lock transitive dependencies or prove the install is governed by committed project state. Version-pinned forms may perhaps be reasonable to downgrade to lower-severity or pedantic findings.

### Additional context

As noted in the #2061's comments, this is likely impossible to comprehensively detect for some ecosystems strictly via static _workflow_ analysis. 

In particular, `{npmx, npm exec, bunx, bun x}` can use locally available package installations in `node_modules`;  this command shape, although typically indicative of an adhoc install, is safe if the package is listed in a lockfile and  _and_ a lockfile-governed install occurs in the job (via e.g., `{npm,bun} ci`) prior to bin execution. Similarly, commands such as `pip install -r requirements.txt` may or may not be dangerous depending on the comprehensiveness of `requirements.txt ` (i.e., does `requirements.txt` constitute a full dependency tree resolution with fully-pinned, hash-checked package versions?). 

From workflow YAML alone, zizmor cannot prove whether these command invocations are dangerous. To correctly disambiguate these cases would require collection and inspection of ecosystem manifest/lockfiles, which seems currently out of scope for this project. #20161 reverted handling for the ambiguous npm cases entirely to avoid false positives, but the long-term direction here may be worth revisiting; perhaps these are still worth flagging (even without inspecting relevant non-YAML files) via pedantic/auditor persona or low confidence findings.

(More broadly, this seems like it can and will run into the same complexity as `use-trusted-publishing`: it's difficult to support security analysis for the usage of many diverse package managers , and to handle them with full accuracy requires (1) re-implementing non-trivial amounts of package manager-specific logic into zizmor, which sucks and may be subject to version drift, and (2) examining ecosystem/package manager specific files outside of zizmor's scope. This is sad.)
title: Feature: Extend `adhoc-packages` audit to other common package managers
